Animosity

/uh-NIM-uh-tee/ — rhymes with celebrity · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Animosity is a strong feeling of hostility or hatred toward someone.

She could barely hide her animosity toward her rival.

Worked Example

Two families in the same town had feuded for generations, their animosity so deep that they refused to sit on the same side of the church.

Animosity is distinct from mere anger because it's a sustained, deep-rooted hostility between people in an ongoing relationship. It involves lasting opposition, not just a momentary feeling. The word captures the permanence and intensity of the hatred, making it more precise than anger or dislike.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

antipathy: Antipathy is a settled, instinctive dislike — a feeling you might have toward crowds, snakes, or a person you barely know, often for no reason you could name. Animosity is hotter and more personal: active hostility toward someone, usually grown out of a real history between you.

rancor: Rancor is bitter resentment that quietly festers — it simmers inside for years after an injury, often hidden behind a polite face. Animosity burns in the open: glares, sharp words, visible hostility. Both can last for years, but rancor smolders while animosity flames.

malice: Malice is the desire to deliberately harm someone — it looks ahead to the damage it wants to cause. Animosity is the hostile feeling itself: it can blaze between two people for years without either one ever forming a plan to hurt the other.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

goodwill: warm, friendly feelings wishing someone well

amity: a peaceful, friendly relationship between people

Where it sits · how deep and lasting the hatred is — dislike → bitterness → hostility → animosity

dislike vs. animosity: Dislike is far weaker than animosity — it is only a mild feeling of not caring for someone, while animosity is deep, active hatred.

bitterness vs. animosity: Bitterness is stronger than simple dislike but still weaker than animosity, because bitterness simmers quietly inside while animosity burns as open hostility toward someone.

hostility vs. animosity: Hostility is intense, but animosity is stronger still — animosity is hostility that has hardened into deep, lasting hatred toward a particular person.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — anim

Root — anim: spirit, mind, life, courage (Latin)

Suffix — -osity

Suffix — -osity: the state of being full of

Put it together

Put it together: The Latin root anim means 'spirit, mind, or courage,' and -osity means 'the state of being full of,' so animosity literally means being full of heated spirit. That fiery, spirited energy came to describe a strong feeling of hostility or hatred aimed at someone.

Use the root in a new word: animate

Use the root in a new word: animate: The puppeteer seemed to animate the wooden marionette, filling it with so much spirit and life that it appeared to breathe.

Word Choice

neutral

Animosity goes deeper than anger or dislike. Use it when hostility is intense, long-lasting, and central to how two people relate. For a quick moment of anger, the plain word 'anger' or 'dislike' works better.
